description: The Wood Blewit (Lepista nuda, also placed in Clitocybe/Collybia and historically in Tricholoma) is a medium-to-large agaric recognizable by its lilac to violet-blue coloration when young. The cap is smooth, domed becoming flattened, about 5-15 cm across, lilac-tinged fading to tan or buff-brown with age and drying. The crowded, sinuate gills and the fibrous, often bulbous-based stem share the violet hue when fresh. The flesh is thick with a distinctive sweetish, fruity-perfumed odour often likened to frozen orange juice. It is a late-season mushroom, fruiting from autumn into winter and tolerant of light frost, typically in troops or arcs/rings in leaf litter, compost, and humus-rich ground in both deciduous and coniferous woodland as well as gardens and hedgerows. Crucially for identification, the spore print is pale pinkish to pinkish-buff. A popular edible that must be cooked thoroughly, it has toxic lilac/purple lookalikes among the Cortinarius webcaps (separated chiefly by rusty-brown spore print and a cortina) and can be confused, when old or faded, with small white muscarine-containing Clitocybe.
edibilityNotes: Edible and well regarded, but ONLY after thorough cooking (at least about 15-20 minutes). Raw or undercooked specimens contain heat-labile compounds that cause gastrointestinal upset; never eat raw. A minority of people experience indigestion or allergic reaction even when it is properly cooked, so eat only a small amount the first time and avoid alcohol with an unfamiliar batch. Always confirm the pale pinkish to pinkish-buff spore print, the lack of a cortina, and the lack of a white spore print before eating: rusty-brown spores with a cobwebby cortina indicate a Cortinarius webcap (some contain the deadly nephrotoxin orellanine), and a white spore print on a small pale specimen may indicate a muscarine-containing Clitocybe.
distribution: Widespread across temperate regions of the Northern Hemisphere, including Europe and North America; also introduced and naturalized in parts of Australia.

dangerousLookalikes.name: Cortinarius webcaps (purple/lilac species)
dangerousLookalikes.note: DEADLY potential. Several purple/violet Cortinarius species resemble young blewits but have a RUSTY-BROWN spore print (vs. pale pink in Lepista nuda) and a cortina (cobweb-like partial veil) that leaves rusty fibres on the stem. Members of the orellanine-containing group (e.g. the C. rubellus / C. orellanus complex) cause delayed, often fatal kidney failure with onset days after ingestion. Spore print colour plus the cortina are the decisive separators.

dangerousLookalikes.name: Violet webcap (Cortinarius violaceus)
dangerousLookalikes.note: Deep violet throughout with a dry, scaly cap, a cortina, and a rusty-brown spore print. Not in the deadly orellanine group but not recommended for eating; the rusty spores and cortina distinguish it from the pink-spored, cortina-free blewit.

dangerousLookalikes.name: Ivory/fool's funnel (Clitocybe rivulosa / C. dealbata)
dangerousLookalikes.note: Small white-to-buff funnel mushrooms that can be confused with old or faded blewits, especially in grass and on lawns. They contain dangerous amounts of muscarine (sweating, salivation, tearing within ~15-30 min; deaths recorded) and give a WHITE spore print rather than pinkish-buff. Size, lack of lilac tones, and white spores separate them.

dangerousLookalikes.name: Lilac fibrecap (Inocybe geophylla var. lilacina)
dangerousLookalikes.note: A small lilac mushroom, much smaller than a blewit, with a conical/umbonate cap, dull clay-brown spore print, and toxic muscarine. Size and brown spores separate it.
